extracted.intended_audience: NIH program officers, peer reviewers, research administrators, and researchers studying funding equity and peer-review processes
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical analysis of NIH R01 application stages (2011–2015) to identify where racial disparities in award rates arise and how applicants' topic choices contribute. Focuses on triage, scoring, programmatic funding decisions, and topic-cluster award-rate baselines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission (which proposals are sent in)
rubrics_metrics.description: Which proposals applicants choose to submit (the applicant-driven selection of topics and proposals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant behavior and topic preferences shape the pool of applications; disparities can begin at this entry stage if underrepresented groups disproportionately propose topics with lower award rates. Assessing rubrics should account for differential submission patterns (e.g., AA/B applicants proposing more community/population health projects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision to discuss (triage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an application makes it past triage into the discussed set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hoppe et al. find disparities at the triage stage — applications from AA/B scientists are less likely to be discussed. Rubrics and reviewer guidance should examine criteria used for triage decisions and whether they systematically disadvantage certain topic types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact score assignment (reviewer numeric rating)
rubrics_metrics.description: The numeric impact/priority score assigned by peer reviewers after discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disparities also appear in impact scores. The study suggests that reviewer scoring standards (e.g., perceived rigor, enthusiasm) vary by topic, so rubrics should clarify scoring interpretations across topic areas to avoid differential application of standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding decision by program staff and council (programmatic selection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Programmatic and council-level decisions that determine which scored applications receive awards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even after peer review, programmatic choices affect award outcomes. Rubrics for funding decisions should make explicit how program priorities interact with topic-cluster award rates and ensure transparency about any adjustments made for topic balance or portfolio considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topic choice (which subject areas applicants choose)
rubrics_metrics.description: The research topic or cluster an application is assigned to or categorized under.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hoppe et al. show topic choice is a previously unstudied stage that contributes substantially to award disparities; rubrics need to acknowledge topic-cluster effects and avoid treating topic selection neutrally when baseline award rates differ across clusters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Award rate by topic cluster (baseline funding probability)
rubrics_metrics.description: The baseline award rate associated with each topic cluster across all applicants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different topic clusters have markedly different award rates (e.g., molecular/basic work has higher award rates than community/population health). Evaluation frameworks should incorporate or adjust for these baseline differences, otherwise they will reproduce observed disparities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer enthusiasm/rigor toward applied/translational/health-disparities work
rubrics_metrics.description: Tendency of reviewers to apply higher rigor standards or show lower enthusiasm for applied/translational and health-disparities research compared with basic/molecular work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study implies reviewers treat applied work more skeptically; rubrics should include explicit guidance to calibrate expectations and value applied/translational outcomes appropriately to prevent systematic devaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field-dependent interpretation of 'Significance'
rubrics_metrics.description: The notion that the NIH review criterion 'significance' is interpreted differently across fields and topic types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Significance appears to be judged in field-dependent ways that disadvantage applied or population-level research. Rubrics should define significance consistently across topic areas or provide topic-specific guidance to ensure fair application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodology preference (mechanistic vs. observational)
rubrics_metrics.description: Preference among reviewers for mechanistic/experimental methodologies over observational or population-level methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological preferences can compound topic-based disparities because certain topics rely on observational or community-level methods. Evaluation rubrics should explicitly value appropriate methodologies for the research question and guard against implicit methodological hierarchies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust rubrics for topic-cluster baseline award rates or justify them
rubrics_metrics.description: Requirement that any rubric not be neutral to topic-cluster award-rate baselines — either adjust for them or transparently justify why some clusters receive lower investment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hoppe et al. argue that failing to account for topic-cluster baselines will replicate disparities; rubric designers should either equalize cluster funding rates, weight evaluations to counteract baseline differences, or provide transparent, evidence-based justification for differential investment across topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topic representation among applicant groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Patterns of which topics are over- or under-represented among specific applicant groups (e.g., AA/B applicants propose more community/population-level, health-disparities, patient-centered outcomes, behavioral intervention topics; fewer basic/molecular topics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding representation patterns is necessary for interpreting disparities: evaluation frameworks should consider how representation interacts with cluster-level award rates and whether selection effects at the applicant level drive observed funding gaps.
